05.imageBrief: Separate namespace authority, forwarding and supported delegation; avoid looping catch-all rules.
learningNotes: Assign distinct AWS and corporate namespace authority and forward each suffix toward its owner.
Avoid sending the same suffix back and forth. Supported Resolver delegation modes differ from simple conditional forwarding.
05.decisionCue: Give each suffix one authoritative owner.

05.title: Resolver endpoint security, capacity and AZ resilience
05.imageBrief: UDP/TCP 53, stateful SG/stateless NACL response paths, multi-AZ IPs, capacity and health.
learningNotes: Inbound endpoint SG permits DNS from forwarders; outbound endpoint SG permits DNS to target servers. Stateful return is tracked.
NACL query/ephemeral response paths, TCP/UDP53, multi-AZ endpoint IPs, target redundancy and capacity monitoring are separate requirements.
05.decisionCue: Test both DNS transports and AZ failure.

05.title: Share Resolver rules across accounts with AWS RAM
05.imageBrief: Central rule ownership and consumer associations; connectivity and authorization remain distinct.
learningNotes: The network account can share forwarding rules using AWS RAM; workload VPCs associate them and use the owner endpoint.
Sharing does not grant private-zone visibility or app connectivity. Endpoint-to-target routes and security remain required.
05.decisionCue: Share policy with explicit consumer association.

05.title: Route 53 Profiles for consistent multi-VPC DNS
05.imageBrief: Bundle supported zone/rule/DNS Firewall associations and distribute with RAM; regional scope and precedence.
learningNotes: Regional Route 53 Profiles bundle supported private-zone associations, Resolver rules, DNS Firewall, logging and DNS settings for VPCs/accounts.
Local associations/settings can take precedence. PrivateLink interface VPC endpoint DNS integration is distinct from Resolver endpoints.
05.decisionCue: Verify effective configuration per VPC.

05.title: Resolve PrivateLink service names from hybrid networks
05.imageBrief: Private DNS, inbound endpoint forwarding, endpoint reachability and security; avoid application IP hardcoding.
learningNotes: Hybrid clients resolve configured service private DNS through an inbound endpoint, then connect separately to the interface endpoint private IP.
Check DNS view, VPN/DX routes, endpoint SG/service port and provider service state; avoid hardcoded ENI addresses.
05.decisionCue: Resolve privately, then validate the connection.

05.title: DNS Firewall: domain filtering and policy evaluation
05.imageBrief: Domain lists, priority/actions, alerts and failure behavior; DNS policy differs from packet inspection.
learningNotes: DNS Firewall evaluates lower numeric association/rule priorities first; ALLOW/BLOCK terminate matching evaluation while ALERT continues.
Default failure mode is closed. Query logs reveal decisions; DNS filtering does not replace egress controls or inspect all third-party encrypted DNS.
05.decisionCue: Use DNS filtering with network egress controls.

05.title: Resolver query logs and DNS observability
05.imageBrief: Query metadata, destinations, limits/cache effects, logging policy and troubleshooting correlation.
learningNotes: Regional Resolver query logging can send data to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose; confirm association and destination permissions.
Cached responses are not logged as new unique queries. Public-zone query logging is separate, and DNS logs are not packet capture.
05.decisionCue: Correlate logs with cache and client behavior.

05.title: Alias, CNAME, apex records and delegation
05.imageBrief: Use supported alias targets, CNAME constraints and public delegation; private delegation is separate.
learningNotes: Alias supports eligible AWS targets/same-zone records and zone-apex use subject to target/type constraints; CNAME maps to another DNS name and cannot be apex.
NS delegation changes authoritative ownership of a subdomain. Same-zone alias type must match its target record; ALB aliases use supported A/AAAA.
05.decisionCue: Choose record shape and authority separately.

05.title: DNS health checks and private application failover
05.imageBrief: Public checker reachability, CloudWatch-alarm health checks, alias target health and readiness limits.
learningNotes: Public Route 53 health checkers cannot directly probe private IPs; private failover can use metric/alarm-data-stream health checks or supported target health.
SetAlarmState does not force health-check state. Test readiness, missing data, all-unhealthy behavior, capacity and caching.
05.decisionCue: Use a reachable and meaningful health signal.

05.title: Route 53 routing policies, TTL and controlled shifts
05.imageBrief: Latency/weighted/failover/location policy decisions and health evaluation; cache affects visibility.
learningNotes: Choose simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation, geoproximity or multivalue according to the required decision and supported zone/record scope.
IP-based routing additionally uses configured client CIDR collections where supported. Weights affect DNS answers, not exact request percentages; TTL and health behavior matter.
05.decisionCue: Choose routing behavior, then account for caching.

05.title: Multi-Region private DNS and Resolver architecture
05.imageBrief: Regional endpoints/rules, zone associations and resilience; private backend connectivity and client entry.
learningNotes: A private hosted zone can associate VPCs across Regions; Resolver endpoints, rules, Profiles and hybrid paths are regional dependencies.
Deploy regional resilience explicitly, test cached answers and avoid unintended central-Region dependency.
05.decisionCue: Treat regional DNS paths as regional dependencies.

05.title: DNSSEC signing versus Resolver validation
05.imageBrief: Public-zone signing and chain of trust vs query validation; private scope limitations and SERVFAIL.
learningNotes: Public-zone signing and Resolver validation are distinct: KSK signs DNSKEY record set; ZSK signs zone record sets, with parent DS establishing trust.
DNSSEC authenticates/integrity-checks DNS, not encryption. Broken chains can cause SERVFAIL; monitor KMS/signing and plan safe rollover.
05.decisionCue: Validate the full DNSSEC chain of trust.

05.title: Troubleshoot timeout, NXDOMAIN, NODATA and SERVFAIL
05.imageBrief: Use caller/resolver/zone/rule/cache/log evidence; isolate security, DNSSEC and forwarding faults.
learningNotes: Use timeout, NXDOMAIN, NODATA and SERVFAIL as evidence with multiple possible causes.
Reproduce same caller/resolver/type; inspect effective zone/rule, cache, DNSSEC, firewall and upstream logs before changing routes.
05.decisionCue: Reproduce the exact caller, resolver and type.

05.title: Scenario: resilient multi-account hybrid DNS
05.imageBrief: Apply namespaces, zones, inbound/outbound rules, shared policy, logging, failure tests and cost tradeoffs.
learningNotes: Design distinct namespaces, regional inbound/outbound endpoints, private-zone/Profiles associations and shared suffix rules for each client view.
Validate DNS and app connectivity separately, including logs, policy, loop prevention, endpoint/AZ/Region failure and cost/retention.
05.decisionCue: Test both directions and every client view.

learningNotes: Validate the selected design against latency, security, routing and resilience requirements.

06.title: BGP policy: choose each direction
learningNotes: Your router controls traffic toward AWS; AWS selects paths toward your advertised networks.
For equal-length prefixes on private and transit VIFs, supported local-preference communities influence AWS path choice.
Use AS-path policy carefully; longest-prefix matching can override a less-specific backup.
Test both directions and failover; do not assume symmetry.

06.title: Direct Connect resilience: separate failure domains
learningNotes: Separate customer routers, power and access circuits.
Use independent AWS devices and multiple Direct Connect locations for location-failure protection.
A second circuit through the same provider conduit may share the same failure.
Test loss of a device, circuit and location; validate surviving capacity.

06.title: LAG: more capacity is not location diversity
learningNotes: LACP aggregates dedicated connections at a single Direct Connect endpoint.
Members share bandwidth characteristics and endpoint failure exposure.
Set minimum active links to define when the logical group remains operational.
Distribute flows across members; a single flow is not guaranteed the aggregate bandwidth.

06.title: Direct Connect backup: design the degraded mode
learningNotes: Use independent Direct Connect paths or an internet VPN backup according to requirements.
Advertise and select routes deliberately; a more-specific route can defeat the intended primary path.
Size backup throughput for critical workloads and defer noncritical transfers if needed.
Measure route convergence, application reconnection and recovery during a real failover test.

06.title: Encryption: identify the protected boundary
learningNotes: TLS protects application sessions between their TLS endpoints.
IPsec protects routed traffic between VPN tunnel endpoints, including supported VPN-over-Direct-Connect designs.
MACsec provides point-to-point Layer2 protection on supported Direct Connect links; it is not application end-to-end encryption.
Direct Connect is not encrypted by default. Select protection for the actual compliance boundary.

06.title: Private IP VPN: encrypted overlay on private transport
06.imageBrief: An overlay still needs an underlay
learningNotes: Private IP Site-to-Site VPN can run over Direct Connect using a transit VIF, Direct Connect gateway and Transit Gateway.
The VPN endpoints use private addressing; the IPsec tunnels carry protected application traffic.
Underlay reachability and overlay route advertisements have distinct jobs.
Avoid recursive routing and verify VPN capacity, feature compatibility and failover.
06.decisionCue: An overlay still needs an underlay

06.title: Transit Gateway Connect: integrate SD-WAN
06.imageBrief: GRE carries traffic; BGP exchanges routes
learningNotes: Connect attachments use a supported transport attachment such as VPC or Direct Connect.
Connect peers use GRE tunnels and BGP for appliance integration.
GRE does not provide encryption. Protect the transport separately when required.
Plan multiple peers, appliance resilience and routes in both directions.
06.decisionCue: GRE carries traffic; BGP exchanges routes

06.title: Hybrid operations: prove the complete path
learningNotes: Check physical link, VIF, BGP session and prefix visibility before application policy.
Inspect VPN tunnel metrics and logs, route tables, flow logs and customer-device counters.
Small packets working while large transfers stall can indicate MTU or MSS problems.
Test realistic workloads during failover; record convergence, packet loss and recovery.

06.title: Compute placement: put constraints first
learningNotes: AWS Regions provide broad managed-service choices and regional resilience options.
Local Zones place supported resources near users while depending on a parent Region.
Outposts place AWS-managed infrastructure in your facility; site readiness and regional connectivity matter.
Customer-managed on-premises compute gives local control with greater operational responsibility.

06.title: Outposts: local compute with regional ties
learningNotes: AWS supplies and manages supported Outposts infrastructure; customers provide site power, space and connectivity.
Run supported AWS workloads near local systems and data.
The service link connects the Outpost to its parent Region for management and service communication.
During disconnects, some existing local workloads continue; regional dependencies and management operations can be impaired.

06.title: Outposts racks: two networking roles
learningNotes: The service link provides connectivity back to the parent Region and carries the control-plane path.
The local gateway connects rack subnets with the on-premises network.
Configure routing, addressing and BGP with the customer network; verify supported routing modes.
Outposts servers use local network interfaces rather than the rack local gateway model.

06.title: Local Zones: nearby resources, regional dependencies
06.imageBrief: Lower latency needs a full path
learningNotes: Enable a supported Local Zone and create a subnet there as an extension of your VPC.
Place supported compute and storage close to users or local systems.
Service availability and instance choices vary by location; validate before designing.
Keep regional services, data paths, failure recovery and cross-zone transfer in the latency and cost model.
06.decisionCue: Lower latency needs a full path

06.title: EKS Anywhere: Kubernetes you operate
learningNotes: Run Kubernetes on supported customer-managed infrastructure using EKS Anywhere tooling.
The customer operates control-plane and worker infrastructure, networking, storage, upgrades and backups.
Plan local image registries, identity, DNS and package access for restricted environments.
EKS Anywhere is different from regional EKS with hybrid nodes; their control-plane locations differ.

06.title: ECS Anywhere: external hosts, AWS orchestration
learningNotes: Register supported external servers or VMs with Systems Manager and the ECS agent.
Use ECS to manage supported tasks on external capacity; provision and maintain the hosts yourself.
Inbound connectivity, host networking, storage and load balancing need an explicit design.
During connectivity loss, existing tasks may continue; cloud scheduling and management are impaired.

06.title: Disconnected operation: map every dependency
learningNotes: Inventory identity, DNS, secrets, registries, databases and external APIs used by the workload.
Classify what continues locally, what degrades and what requires regional connectivity.
Cache or replicate only where semantics, security and staleness limits permit.
Test disconnect and reconnection, including reconciliation, credential expiry and recovery.

06.title: Hybrid case: justify the whole design
learningNotes: Requirement: local low-latency processing, resilient AWS connectivity and encrypted sensitive traffic.
Choose local compute by operational ownership and service dependencies; use diverse network paths.
Specify encryption endpoints, routing preferences, backup capacity and access controls.
Prove application recovery with device, circuit and regional-dependency failures; document tradeoffs.

06.title: VPN CloudHub: connect remote sites
learningNotes: Multiple Site-to-Site VPN connections can share a virtual private gateway to connect remote sites.
Use BGP with unique customer ASNs and nonoverlapping site prefixes.
The virtual private gateway can re-advertise site routes to other sites.
This is remote-site connectivity, not transitive VPC peering. Compare with Transit Gateway as the network grows.

06.title: Client VPN: identity, routes and authorization
learningNotes: Authenticate users with a supported method: mutual certificates, Active Directory or federated SAML.
Authorization rules specify destination access; authentication alone does not grant network reachability.
Configure target-network connectivity, endpoint routes and destination security controls.
Plan client addressing, DNS, connection logging and highly available target connectivity.

06.title: Client VPN: choose the traffic path
learningNotes: Split tunnel installs endpoint routes on the client; matching traffic uses the VPN.
Full tunnel sends client traffic through the VPN; provide a deliberate internet-egress design.
Reach peered VPCs or on-premises networks only with complete routes, authorization and return connectivity.
Transit Gateway integration is supported; check its endpoint-specific requirements and authorization limitations.

06.title: Direct Connect SiteLink: site-to-site transport
learningNotes: SiteLink enables supported on-premises sites to exchange traffic through Direct Connect locations.
Enable SiteLink on supported private or transit VIFs associated with the same Direct Connect gateway.
The site-to-site path can bypass AWS Regions; compare route policy and WAN requirements.
SiteLink does not remove customer access-circuit failures or provide automatic end-to-end application encryption.

07.title: EC2 selection: start with the bottleneck
07.imageBrief: Match resources to measured demand
learningNotes: Compute-optimized fits CPU-heavy work; memory-optimized fits large working sets.
Storage-optimized targets local I/O; accelerated instances suit workloads that use their GPU or other accelerator.
General-purpose balances resources. Check network and EBS limits as well as vCPU and RAM.
Benchmark representative traffic; the instance family name is a starting point, not proof of performance.
CPU family examples include C, memory R, balanced M, local-I/O I, and GPU G/P; actual capabilities depend on generation and size. Evaluate EBS throughput, network packet rate and memory pressure.
07.decisionCue: Match resources to measured demand

07.title: Burstable compute: understand the credit budget
07.imageBrief: Short bursts are different from sustained demand
learningNotes: Burstable instances earn CPU credits below baseline and spend them above baseline.
Standard mode is constrained when credits run out; Unlimited mode can incur surplus-credit charges.
Monitor credit balance and sustained CPU demand before choosing a smaller instance.
Check architecture and software compatibility when comparing Graviton and x86; price-performance requires testing.

Unlimited mode bills surplus credits when sustained use exceeds the baseline over the applicable credit accounting period. Validate Linux/Arm binaries, container images and native dependencies for Graviton.
07.decisionCue: Short bursts are different from sustained demand

07.title: EC2 lifecycle: know what survives
07.imageBrief: Memory, storage and identity have different lifetimes
learningNotes: Reboot restarts the guest OS and clears volatile runtime state; EBS and instance-store data normally remain.
Stop/start preserves EBS volumes but loses RAM and instance-store data; the underlying host can change.
Hibernation saves RAM to an encrypted EBS root volume on supported configurations; capacity and prerequisites matter.
Termination removes the instance. EBS retention depends on delete-on-termination settings; protect important data separately.

An auto-assigned public IPv4 address can change after stop/start; private addressing and Elastic IP behavior differ. Hibernation requires a supported EBS-backed configuration with sufficient encrypted root-volume space.
07.decisionCue: Memory, storage and identity have different lifetimes

07.title: Repeatable launches: build a replacement, not a pet
07.imageBrief: An AMI and launch template define the starting point
learningNotes: An AMI supplies the boot image; a versioned launch template defines instance launch settings.
Bootstrap with user data or prepared images. Scripts must handle retries and avoid embedding long-lived secrets.
Use an instance profile for AWS access and require IMDSv2 where supported.
Updating a launch template does not update running instances; roll replacements with health checks.
07.decisionCue: An AMI and launch template define the starting point

07.title: Stateless compute: make replacement safe
07.imageBrief: Externalize the state that must survive
learningNotes: Keep sessions and durable application data outside an individual EC2 instance.
Use suitable shared databases, caches and storage with their own resilience and consistency design.
Local caches and temporary files are acceptable only when rebuilding or losing them is safe.
A load balancer and multiple AZs help availability only when dependencies and replacement capacity also survive.
07.decisionCue: Externalize the state that must survive

07.title: EC2 purchasing: separate discount from capacity
07.imageBrief: Choose the commitment around the workload
learningNotes: On-Demand suits flexible usage; Savings Plans and Reserved Instances trade commitment for eligible discounts.
A discount commitment does not always reserve capacity. Regional Reserved Instances do not provide a capacity reservation.
Use eligible zonal reservations or On-Demand Capacity Reservations when capacity assurance is required.
Spot uses spare capacity and can be interrupted. Match purchase options to workload tolerance and availability needs.

Savings Plans commit eligible usage spend; Reserved Instances vary by class, scope, platform and payment option. Zonal RI capacity benefits apply only to matching attributes. On-Demand Capacity Reservations incur charges even when unused; discounts may apply to eligible matching usage.
07.decisionCue: Choose the commitment around the workload

07.title: Spot design: expect interruption
07.imageBrief: Recovery is part of the application
learningNotes: Use diversified instance types and Availability Zones with a capacity-aware allocation strategy.
Checkpoint useful progress to durable storage; make retries idempotent and drain work when possible.
Interruption notices and rebalance recommendations help but are not a guaranteed grace period for all interruptions.
Capacity Rebalancing can launch replacements proactively; it cannot guarantee available capacity or prevent interruption.

Spot interruption warnings are best effort; hibernation begins immediately without the usual two-minute lead. Use price-capacity-optimized allocation where appropriate; stopping a request and terminating running instances are distinct lifecycle actions.
07.decisionCue: Recovery is part of the application

07.title: Tenancy: isolation and licensing are separate choices
07.imageBrief: Dedicated does not automatically mean compliant
learningNotes: Shared tenancy runs instances on hardware shared with other customers.
Dedicated Instances provide dedicated hardware isolation without the host-level placement control of Dedicated Hosts.
Dedicated Hosts expose physical host allocation and placement controls useful for some socket or core licensing models.
Verify license terms, supported configurations, host recovery and cost before selecting tenancy.
07.decisionCue: Dedicated does not automatically mean compliant

07.title: Placement: choose the failure domain deliberately
07.imageBrief: Performance and hardware isolation have tradeoffs
learningNotes: Cluster placement groups place supported instances close together within one Availability Zone for low-latency workloads.
Spread placement groups separate instances across distinct hardware; check limits and the supported spread level.
Partition placement groups separate groups of instances across distinct hardware partitions for distributed systems.
Placement is not data replication or Multi-AZ recovery. Plan capacity, replica placement and application resilience separately.

Rack-level spread groups have a per-AZ instance limit; partition groups support up to seven partitions per AZ. Applications should place replicas across partitions using placement metadata. Changing group placement can require stop/start and compatible capacity; cluster placement is not a guarantee of one rack.
07.decisionCue: Performance and hardware isolation have tradeoffs

07.title: EC2 networking: match the workload and software
07.imageBrief: ENA and EFA serve different needs
learningNotes: ENA provides enhanced networking on supported instances; performance depends on instance limits and configuration.
EFA supports low-latency communication for suitable HPC and ML applications using supported libraries.
EFA OS-bypass traffic requires supported software and same-AZ placement; validate security-group and platform requirements.
Inspect bandwidth, packet rate, latency and traffic patterns; a larger advertised bandwidth does not fix every bottleneck.

ENA uses hardware-assisted networking; EFA OS-bypass uses supported libfabric-based stacks such as MPI or NCCL. Check Linux support, compatible instance types, same-AZ requirements and self-referencing security-group rules rather than assuming any application gains EFA acceleration.
07.decisionCue: ENA and EFA serve different needs

07.title: HPC: the slowest layer limits the job
07.imageBrief: Compute, communication, storage and scheduling must fit
learningNotes: Tightly coupled jobs need fast inter-node communication; independent jobs scale differently.
Choose storage for the access pattern: durable objects, shared files, block storage or disposable local scratch.
FSx for Lustre can support parallel file access and S3 integration; data staging and persistence still need a plan.
Compare managed job scheduling with cluster tooling such as ParallelCluster; validate data movement, checkpoints and recovery.

AWS Batch supports managed scheduling including eligible EC2 multi-node parallel jobs; assess supported capacity options. ParallelCluster automates HPC cluster provisioning and scheduler configuration. DataSync, Direct Connect and other current data-transfer options are covered in hybrid/storage/migration modules; do not treat discontinued transfer offerings from older PDFs as current recommendations.
07.decisionCue: Compute, communication, storage and scheduling must fit

07.title: Auto Scaling groups: define the safe operating range
07.imageBrief: Desired capacity is a target, not a guarantee
learningNotes: Minimum, desired and maximum capacity bound how the group manages instances.
Use supported subnets across Availability Zones and a reproducible launch template.
Capacity shortages, quotas, launch failures and dependency limits can prevent the desired capacity from becoming healthy.
Auto Scaling replaces instances; application architecture must make replacement and zone failure safe.
07.decisionCue: Desired capacity is a target, not a guarantee

07.title: Target tracking: scale on useful per-instance demand
07.imageBrief: Choose a metric that responds to capacity
learningNotes: Target tracking adjusts capacity to keep a suitable utilization metric near a target.
CPU, ALB requests per target or well-designed custom utilization metrics can fit different workloads.
Raw queue length is not enough for proportional target tracking; backlog per worker can express useful demand.
Allow warmup and validate scale-in behavior; adding instances helps only if they relieve the actual bottleneck.

For several target tracking policies, scale-out can occur if any policy requires it; scale-in requires all scale-in-enabled target tracking policies to agree. Backlog per worker target can be derived from acceptable processing latency divided by average processing time; validate units and idempotency.
07.decisionCue: Choose a metric that responds to capacity

07.title: Step scaling: react to the size of the breach
07.imageBrief: Alarm-driven adjustments need tuning
learningNotes: Step scaling changes capacity based on how far a metric breaches configured thresholds.
Simple scaling uses a single adjustment and cooldown behavior; prefer target tracking or step scaling where appropriate.
Avoid conflicting policies and aggressive scale-in that removes capacity before demand stabilizes.
Test thresholds, adjustment size and warmup using realistic bursts, including noisy and missing metrics.
07.decisionCue: Alarm-driven adjustments need tuning

07.title: Scheduled and predictive scaling: prepare ahead
07.imageBrief: Known events and forecast demand are different
learningNotes: Scheduled actions change capacity bounds or desired capacity at known times.
Predictive scaling forecasts recurring demand and can prepare capacity before the forecast rise.
Combine proactive capacity with dynamic scaling for unexpected demand; forecasts do not guarantee accuracy.
Account for time zones, startup time, maximum capacity and changes in workload patterns.
07.decisionCue: Known events and forecast demand are different

07.title: Warmup and warm pools: readiness is not one timer
07.imageBrief: Prepare capacity without misleading the controller
learningNotes: Default instance warmup helps scaling policies account for instances whose metrics are not yet representative.
Health-check grace periods delay certain health-check replacement decisions; they do not prove application readiness.
Warm pools keep prepared instances outside active service to reduce startup delay; retained state and costs depend on pool configuration.
Use lifecycle hooks for initialization and verify that restored instances are actually ready before serving traffic.

Cooldown, default instance warmup and health-check grace period serve different purposes. Warm pools can use supported stopped, running or hibernated configurations, with storage/compute cost and startup implications.
07.decisionCue: Prepare capacity without misleading the controller

07.title: Lifecycle hooks: make transitions deliberate
07.imageBrief: A bounded wait gives automation time
learningNotes: Launch hooks can pause an instance while initialization, validation or registration tasks run.
Termination hooks can support draining, cleanup and log collection before normal termination proceeds.
Send heartbeats or complete the lifecycle action; timeouts and failure results require an explicit policy.
Hooks do not guarantee protection from Spot interruption. Keep cleanup bounded and make processing retry-safe.
07.decisionCue: A bounded wait gives automation time

07.title: Instance refresh: roll a new launch definition safely
07.imageBrief: A new template is not a completed deployment
learningNotes: Create the desired launch-template version, then use instance refresh to replace existing instances.
Set healthy-capacity limits and warmup so enough ready capacity remains during replacement.
Use supported checkpoints, bake time and alarm-based rollback features to detect deployment problems.
Validate rollback prerequisites and application compatibility; replacing compute does not reverse database changes.

Instance refresh can use skip matching, checkpoints, bake time and supported alarm-triggered rollback. Rollback support depends on a resolvable supported launch-template version; validate limitations for dynamic latest/default versions and AMI references.
07.decisionCue: A new template is not a completed deployment

07.title: Health and recovery: match the check to the failure
07.imageBrief: Infrastructure, guest, storage and application checks differ
learningNotes: System status checks assess underlying infrastructure; instance status checks assess guest reachability.
Attached EBS status checks assess attached volume reachability and I/O capability; application checks require configured HTTP health criteria.
Configure the appropriate Auto Scaling health sources and grace period; a healthy guest does not prove a healthy application.
Supported EC2 recovery can preserve identity after certain system failures. Collect memory and filesystem metrics with agents or custom metrics.

System, instance and attached EBS checks are managed checks; application checks are opt-in HTTP/HTTPS checks. Configure eligible Auto Scaling health sources explicitly. EC2 recovery and Auto Scaling replacement preserve different identity/state properties; recovery is not application repair.
07.decisionCue: Infrastructure, guest, storage and application checks differ

07.title: Scale-in: protect work, not just instance count
07.imageBrief: Graceful removal is an application behavior
learningNotes: Load-balancer deregistration delay lets supported in-flight connections drain within configured limits.
Use scale-in protection for selected instances when appropriate; it does not block every replacement or termination path.
Queue workers should stop accepting new work, finish or checkpoint tasks, and return unfinished work for retry.
Choose termination policy and hooks carefully; test long requests, failures and scale-in during deployments.

Scale-in protection does not prevent Spot interruption, explicit termination or all unhealthy-instance replacement paths. Queue visibility timeout, checkpoints and retries must protect unfinished work.
07.decisionCue: Graceful removal is an application behavior

07.title: Mixed instances: capacity units must mean the same thing
07.imageBrief: Flexibility improves options but adds design checks
learningNotes: A mixed-instances policy can combine eligible instance types and On-Demand or Spot capacity.
Use suitable instance requirements or overrides and ensure the AMI supports the chosen architecture.
Capacity weights can express different units of useful capacity; metrics and scaling targets must use compatible units.
Balance diversification, baseline On-Demand capacity, allocation strategy and interruption recovery.

A hosted AMI for one CPU architecture cannot simply boot on another. Use appropriate launch-template overrides and compatible images when diversifying; weighted capacity changes the meaning of desired units.
07.decisionCue: Flexibility improves options but adds design checks

07.title: EC2 architecture case: prove the bottleneck and recovery
07.imageBrief: Justify every capacity decision
learningNotes: Measure the limiting resource and choose compatible instance families, storage and network features.
Keep durable state external, distribute across AZs and make instances reproducibly replaceable.
Select purchasing and scaling policies around demand shape, startup time and interruption tolerance.
Load-test normal traffic, bursts, scale-in and failures; verify latency, cost, data safety and recovery.
07.decisionCue: Justify every capacity decision

07.title: Precision time: placement for clock accuracy
07.imageBrief: Time accuracy is a distinct requirement
learningNotes: Precision-time placement groups use supported hardware with access to high-precision time sources.
Supported instances can use enhanced Amazon Time Sync capabilities; verify the instance, Region and configuration requirements.
Clock accuracy is different from network latency or hardware failure isolation; choose the placement strategy for the actual requirement.
Measure synchronization and application needs; precision-time placement does not replace replication, backup or Multi-AZ design.

Precision-time placement can provide enhanced local NTP, Linux PTP hardware clock access and hardware packet timestamping on supported configurations. Cluster placement can specify a precision-time parent group where supported; clock accuracy and cluster network locality are separate capabilities.
07.decisionCue: Time accuracy is a distinct requirement
